title: Vesak, the fourth time
hook: Vesak as the schools keep it, side by side

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the practice traditions with one simple, honest line: choose one.

Four scenes, all honoring one person. In a Sri Lankan town, a lit gateway the height of a house shows a story from the Buddha's past lives, and a stall hands out free drinks. In a Japanese temple courtyard, children ladle sweet tea over a tiny statue of a baby with one hand pointing up. In Seoul, a river of paper lotus lanterns moves through the streets at night. In Lhasa, pilgrims walk the circuit around the old city all month long, prayer wheels turning. Different dates, different food, different music. This is your fourth Vesak on the path, so today, instead of standing in one country, stand where you can see them all at once.
screen: `GATEWAYS AND FREE DRINKS.` → `SWEET TEA OVER A BABY.` → `LANTERNS AND A HOLY MONTH.`

segments.voice: Start with Vesak as Theravada lands like Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar keep it: one full moon remembers three things together, the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his passing away. That's your line today: born, awake, gone. Next, the schools that separate them. In Japan, the birth stands on its own, at the flower festival in spring, with the sweet tea and the pointing baby. The awakening has its own day in winter, and the passing its own day too. Korean and Chinese communities also keep the birthday as its own feast, with lanterns and the bathing of a small Buddha statue. Then Tibet, where a whole month, Saga Dawa, is set apart. Its full moon remembers the awakening and the passing, and in some tellings the birth as well. Some Tibetan teachers say that good and harmful actions done in that month carry extra weight. Now set them side by side. The dates differ, the music differs, but underneath, the same thing is said. The Dhammapada has a short verse for it, in Max Müller's words: "Happy is the arising of the awakened." Each school, in its own way, is glad that this person was born, woke up, and taught. And a festival kept side by side isn't a contest over who keeps it best. A lantern in Seoul and a lamp in Colombo are both lit for the same arrival.
screen: `ONE MOON, THREE EVENTS.` · `SEPARATE DAYS IN JAPAN.` · `A HOLY MONTH IN TIBET.` · then, large: `HAPPY IS THE ARISING.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a small lamp, light it safely where you can see it; a phone screen turned low, or the light in the window, will do. For a few breaths think born, a small life arriving; for a few more, awake, eyes open; for a few more, gone, a flame that will one day go out. Then let the words fall away and just watch the light.
Vesak. The full moon on which Theravada Buddhists remember the birth, the awakening and the passing, kept in different ways by different schools. Today's word.
Your line: born, awake, gone. Three events, one full moon, and many lanterns lit. Happy Vesak.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries, Buddhists keep Vesak on a full moon with temple visits, extra precepts, giving and lamps; in Japan, Korea and China the birth is often kept as its own day, and in Tibet the month of Saga Dawa is set apart.

chat.says: Why do Buddhists celebrate Vesak on different days in different countries?
options: Schools mark the birth, awakening and passing differently, but all are glad for the same life.
Each country honors a different Buddha, so the festivals aren't really the same one.
The dates were set by kings long ago, and nobody remembers the real reasons now.
chat.meaning: Theravada lands keep birth, awakening and passing on one full moon; Japan and Tibet set them apart. The dates differ, but each is glad for the same arrival.

Vesak.meaning: the full moon of the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing

Saga Dawa.meaning: the Tibetan holy month of the awakening and passing

Theravada.meaning: the Buddhist school whose scriptures are in Pali
